newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela's Petkoff woos bolsa with straight talk.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela's Petkoff woos bolsa with straight talk.

text.p: Venezuela's Planning Minister Teodoro Petkoff took his characteristic brand of straight talking to the Caracas Stock Exchange Thursday where he urged investors and brokers to have as much confidence in their country as their foreign counterparts.
"Don't allow what happened in Chile, where they woke up to find their territory occupied," Petkoff said in an address at the exchange.

The former communist guerrilla fighter whose incorporation into the government earlier this year has been cited as the turning point in the country's fortunes, said foreign investors were queuing up to invest in many sectors of the economy.
Asked how local investors could compete in the opening up of the economy he said: "All you have to do is shout."
The government would set aside stakes in the forthcoming privatizations of state banks, telephone company CANTV, the aluminum sector and steel company Sidor for the local stock market, he added.
As Petkoff spoke, foreign buying drove stocks on the Caracas Stock Exchange to a fifth successive record.
Those who listened to Petkoff noted that less than one year ago it would have been unthinkable that he would come to the stock market to woo investors.
"It shows how much can change in this country," one said.
While many complained that Petkoff's address lacked specifics, most applauded his direct, honest style.
At one stage, Petkoff recalled his horror at discovering that government offices routinely neglected to pay their telephone and electricity bills.
Under current legislation, utilities are not allowed to cut off services to the public sector even if bills are unpaid.
"This must be changed," Petkoff said. "Those who don't pay must be cut off," he said to loud applause and cheers.
Trading on the Caracas Stock Exchange is dominated by electric utility Electricidad de Caracas to which the state owes more than $30 million in past-due bills.
